title: How to Film Recipe Videos on a Phone | Jupiter
summary: How to film recipe videos on a phone: simple gear, 8 shots, hooks for the first 2 seconds, pacing in the edit and one video for Reels, TikTok and Shorts.
body_markdown:
How to film recipe videos is mostly a planning question. The creators whose videos look effortless usually work from a shot list, shoot every step the same way, and decide the opening before they turn the stove on.


Our point of view: the shot list matters more than the camera. A phone with a plan beats an expensive setup filmed on instinct, and it makes editing take minutes instead of hours.


## What gear do you need to film recipe videos?


You need less than most gear lists suggest. Start with these and upgrade only when one becomes the bottleneck.


Item


Why it matters


Low-cost option


Phone


Shoots sharp vertical video


The phone you already have


Soft light


Keeps food bright without harsh shadows


A window with a sheer curtain


Overhead mount


Steady top-down shots of every step


A tripod with a horizontal arm


Clean surface


Keeps the eye on the food


A board, tile or baking sheet


Cloth and spoon


Fixes drips between takes


Kitchen towel and a small spoon


Turn off overhead room lights while filming. Mixing warm bulbs with daylight gives food an odd color that's hard to fix later.


## How to film recipe videos: the 8-shot structure


Shoot every recipe from the same list. It keeps your videos consistent and means you never get to the edit missing a step.


1.


**The hero shot.**


The finished dish at its best, filmed first while you have energy and clean props, or last when it's fresh.


2.


**Ingredients.**


Everything laid out, so viewers know what to buy.


3.


**The first action.**


Chopping, cracking or measuring, to show the recipe has started.


4.


**The combine.**


Ingredients going into the bowl or pan.


5.


**The change.**


The moment the food transforms: browning, rising, thickening.


6.


**The texture moment.**


A pour, a pull, a crack or a slice.


7.


**The plating.**


The dish going onto a plate or into a bowl.


8.


**The bite or serve.**


A fork, a hand, or a spoonful, so people picture eating it.


Film each shot a little longer than you need. Two extra seconds at the start and end of every clip gives you room to cut cleanly.


## Hooks for the first two seconds


The first two seconds decide whether people keep watching. Open with the most appealing shot, not the start of the method.


Strong openings for food include the finished dish, the texture moment, or a close-up of the step people find surprising. Pair it with a few words on screen, such as the dish name or why it's worth making.


Avoid opening on an empty bowl, a slow pan or your hand reaching into frame. Save the setup for after you've earned attention.

## Editing apps and pacing


Use whatever editor you're fastest in. Most built-in app editors and free mobile editors can trim clips, add text and sync to sound.


Pacing rules that hold up:


-


Cut each step to the shortest clip that still shows what changed.


-


Keep on-screen text short enough to read in one glance.


-


Speed up long waits, such as simmering or proofing, rather than cutting them out.


-


End on the hero shot again, so the last frame makes people want to save it.


Watch the full edit once with the sound off. If the recipe still makes sense, your visuals are doing the work.
